winisd.driver: Dayton Audio DSA215-8; 100 W, amplifier resistance 0.1 Ω, losses Ql 10 / Qa 100 / Qp 100 and WinISD's air, unless a case says otherwise

checks.note: WinISD's “Fsc” field is the −3 dB frequency

cases.title: Ported box at 100 W: every graph (Test 1)
cases.setup: The ported box at 100.08 W (24.3 V), read from each graph's cursor
cases.notes: The shapes match; the absolute level sits a uniform ~0.03 dB (0.35 %) below WinISD and the impedance peaks are up to 0.8 % higher. Simulating from the Bl/Mms/Cms/Rms values stored in the project instead of deriving them from Fs/Qes/Qms/Vas made the agreement worse, so WinISD derives them as we do. The remaining offset is far below anything measurable.

cases.title: Ported box with a high-pass filter (Test 3)
cases.setup: The ported box with a 2nd-order Butterworth high-pass at 25 Hz (read from the project's filters)

cases.title: Ported box with voice-coil inductance (Test 4)
cases.setup: The ported box with “Simulate voice coil inductance” on, Le 1 mH
cases.notes: WinISD models Le as a plain series inductor, as this comparison does. The app's optional L2R2 model goes further (see below).

cases.title: Two drivers in parallel (Test 5)
cases.setup: Two DSA215-8 in parallel in the ported box at 100 W
cases.notes: WinISD applies the amplifier resistance Rg to each driver separately and plots one driver's impedance. The app shares Rg between the drivers and shows the impedance the amplifier sees, so the comparison divides Rg by the number of drivers and multiplies the impedance by it.

cases.title: Ported box with leakage Ql 7 (Test 6)
cases.setup: The ported box with Ql 7 instead of WinISD's default 10

cases.title: 4th-order bandpass (Test 7)
cases.setup: 15 L sealed rear, 20 L front tuned to 50 Hz, 7.5 cm port
cases.notes: WinISD includes leakage between the chambers (Qiclfr = 100); so does the app.

cases.title: 6th-order bandpass (Test 8)
cases.setup: 20 L rear tuned to 35 Hz, 15 L front tuned to 70 Hz, both ported to the outside
cases.notes: This case pins the inter-chamber leak's reference to the driver (R = Q / (ωs·Cas)).

cases.title: Isobaric pairs in a sealed box (Test 9)
cases.setup: Two isobaric pairs (coils in series) in the 10.4 L sealed box, at WinISD's voltage
cases.notes: WinISD wires the two coils of a pair in series, applies Rg to each coil, and sets the voltage as if the pairs were single drivers, V = √(P·Re/Nd), which puts only about half its stated power into the coils. The app keeps the power physical, so the comparison drives both at the same voltage.

cases.title: Isobaric pairs in a ported box (Test 10)
cases.setup: Two isobaric pairs in the 18 L ported box, same conventions as Test 9

cases.title: Dual voice coil driver, coils in series (Test 11)
cases.setup: The DSA215-8 as a DVC driver wired in series (Re 23.6 Ω, Bl 21.2) in the ported box
cases.notes: WinISD stores the driver as wired (Re 23.6 Ω and Bl 21.2 from 5.9 Ω / 10.6 entered for the coils in parallel), then simulates it like any single-coil driver.

cases.title: Passive radiator, 18 L
cases.setup: 1 × DSA270-PR with 50 g added in 18 L (Fb 45.90 Hz)
cases.notes: Box tuning matches exactly, so radiator mass and stiffness are modelled the same way. The remaining difference is **damping near the tuning frequency**: WinISD shows less loss there than the standard lumped loss model (the same model that matches its ported and sealed boxes to 0.01 dB). Moving the loss reference frequencies, scaling the radiator's Qms and removing individual losses were all tried; none reproduces both WinISD PR boxes, so WinISD evidently treats passive-radiator losses differently internally. Real box leakage varies far more than this (Ql 5–20 is typical).

cases.title: Passive radiator, 50 L
cases.setup: 1 × DSA270-PR, no added mass, in 50 L (Fb 38.67 Hz): a high-Q tuning with a dip above it
cases.notes: Right at the tuning peak WinISD shows less damping than the standard loss model (−1.21 against −1.70 dB): the same passive-radiator damping difference as the 18 L box.

checks.note: the tuning peak: see the known difference

cases.title: Passive radiator excursion at 100 W (Test 2)
cases.setup: The 18 L + 50 g PR box at 100.1 W: cone and PR excursion graphs
cases.notes: Away from the tuning the agreement matches the ported box (0.35–0.5 %). Close to Fb, WinISD's lighter PR damping shows up again: a slightly deeper cone dip and a little more PR travel. The dip and bump frequencies agree within 0.05 Hz.

hornresp.driver: Dayton Audio DSA215-8 (Le 1 mH) at 2.83 V in half space, Hornresp's air (c 344 m/s, ρ 1.205 kg/m³), SPL from radiated power
hornresp.notes:
The line's resonances fall on the same frequencies as Hornresp's. The only large SPL differences are at the bottom of deep nulls: the same frequency, a different depth (a few hundredths of a hertz move the bottom of a 40 dB null by many dB), which is why SPL is held to its mean and 95th percentile rather than its worst point.

What the comparison found and fixed:

- **The cone's mass in lines and horns.** The air on both sides of the cone is modelled explicitly, so the cone carries its bare mass (Mms less the air load), as Hornresp does. Using Mms had counted the rear air mass twice and made impedance peaks up to 10 % low.
- **SPL from radiated power.** Hornresp works SPL out from the power each opening radiates, not from on-axis pressure. The two agree at low frequency and part once the mouth is large next to the wavelength (about 1.7 dB at 500 Hz for an 850 cm² mouth). The app shows on-axis SPL by default; Settings → Line/horn SPL → “From radiated power (like Hornresp)” gives Hornresp's.

Stuffed lines (08 and 09 in the records) aren't automated: Hornresp uses segment filling only in its Loudspeaker Wizard, so they were read off its charts. Acoustic power agreed within about 1 dB from 20 Hz to 1 kHz, and every impedance peak fell at the same frequency (straight TL: 63 Hz / 13.8 Ω against ~63 Hz / ~14.0 Ω). The two fibre models differ, so stuffed lines are judged on the trend.
